blocks.text: Of these animals, Giauhari describes the former as follows: الوبر دويبة اصغر من السنور كحلا اللون لا ذنب لها تدجن في البيوت [al-wabr duwayba aṣghar min al-sinnawr kaḥlā al-lawn lā dhanab lahā tadjun fī al-buyūt], Alwebro is a small animal, smaller than a cat, of dusky colour, without a tail, living in houses. But, as Damir observes, قوله لا ذنب لها اي لا ذنب لها [col. 1005] طويل والا فالوبر له ذنب قصير جدا [qawluhu lā dhanab lahā ay lā dhanab lahā ṭawīl wa-illā fa-l-wabr lahu dhanab qaṣīr jiddan] When he denies that it has a tail, he means that its tail is not long; for alwebro does indeed have a tail, but a very short one. He also states that some call it غنم بني اسرايل [ghanam banī Isrāyil] the sheep of the children of Israel; لان ذنبها مع صغره يشبه الية الخروف [li-anna dhanabahā maʿa ṣigharihi yushbih alyat al-kharūf] because its tail, by its shortness, resembles a lamb's tail ^{(2)}. But in Giauhari it is called زلم [zulam] zulem, for what reason I do not sufficiently know. In the book entitled كفاية المتحفظة [Kifāyat al-mutaḥaffiẓa] we read that الوبر [al-wabr] alwebro is دويبة قريبة من السنور ولها بول يتخثر فيتداوي به الناس [duwayba qarība min al-sinnawr wa-lahā bawl yatakhaththar fa-yatadāwī bihi al-nās] a small animal like a cat, whose urine thickens and is used among the remedies for diseases. Mawardi and Rujiani say that it is an animal في عظم الجرذ الا انه انبل منه والعرب تاكله [fī ʿiẓam al-juradh illā annahu anbal minhu wa-l-ʿArab taʾkuluhu] of the size of a larger mouse, but finer, which the Arabs eat. By others it is described as دويبة سودا في قدر الارنب واكبر من ابن عرس [duwayba sūdā fī qadr al-arnab wa-akbar min ibn ʿirs] a small black animal, approaching the size of a hare, and larger than a weasel. The same animal, as some add, كالارنب يعتلف النبات والبقول [ka-l-arnab yaʿtalif al-nabāt wa-l-buqūl] feeds, like the hare, on herbs and vegetables. I take it to be the marmot, or mountain mouse, which Gesner describes thus: It is more corpulent than a cat, but shorter in the legs, etc. Its colour is for the most part reddish, brighter in some, darker and dusky in others. And Scaliger against Cardano, Exercise 203: They are of the size and fur of badgers, and likewise have almost no tail. He adds that he kept a tame one among the Taurini. And Gesner: I shall describe its natural history, partly as I myself [II, 414] observed it when I kept this animal at home. And Stumpf: Of the wild animals of our part of the world you will scarcely find any that becomes so tame and familiar to man. He had, namely, kept one at home for two years. Pliny, book 8, chapter 37, calls it the Alpine mouse, because it is common in the Alps. But lest anyone think that these mice are peculiar to the Alps, he describes similar ones in Egypt ^{(3)}. Nor is it only for the Arabs that the שפן saphan of Moses is الوبر [al-wabr] alvvebro, or the mountain mouse. For among our own scholars too Junius, who had by no means consulted the Arabs, consistently renders the Hebrew שפן [II, 415] in this way. So too another anonymous writer, of whom Gesner says in the chapter On the Alpine mouse: Saphan, a Hebrew word, etc., a certain learned man among us interprets as the Alpine mouse. Note in passing that the Italian name of the mountain or Alpine mouse, marmota, is found, slightly altered, in two places in Bereschith Rabba. The first is section 17, on the words of Gen. II, 21. The Lord God caused תרדמה thardema (that is, a deep sleep) to fall upon Adam. רב אמר שלש תרדמת הן תרדמת שינה תרדמת נבואה ותרדמת מרמיטה תרדמת שינה ויפול יהוה תרדמה על האדם [col. 1006] וישן תרדמת נבואה ויהי השמש לבא ותרדמה נפלה על אברם תרדמת מרמיטה אין רואה ואין יודע ואין מקיץ כי כלם ישנים כי תרדמת י״ נפלה עליהם Rab said: there are three kinds of deep sleep: the deep sleep of slumber, the deep sleep of prophecy, and the deep sleep of מרמיטה marmita. The deep sleep of slumber, Gen. II, 21: “The Lord God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept. The deep sleep of prophecy, Gen. XV, 12: And when the sun was going down, a deep sleep fell upon Abram. The deep sleep of מרמיטה marmita, 1 Sam. XXVI, 12: There was no one who saw, nor who understood, nor who awoke, but they were all asleep; because a deep sleep from the Lord had fallen upon them.” The other place is section 43, where these same words are repeated on Gen. XV, 12. In both places the word מרמיטה marmita has tormented the interpreters not a little. R. Selomo renders it בהלה, that is, terror and confusion. So too the Scholiast on these passages, and the most distinguished Buxtorf. Baal Aruch renders it marble; as if it were called the sleep of marble, in which we become stupefied like marble or, in general, like stone: as is said of the Egyptians in Exod. XV, 16. ידמו כאבן, let them be still as a stone. Postel: the deep sleep of carrus, or of the vehemence of a more profound sleep. One should read cari, that is, κάρου [karou]. Boderianus, Pomarius and Aquinas emend מרמיטה marmita to דורמיטה dormita, so that it would mean dormitatio [dozing]. Yet our copies consistently read מרמיטה marmita, and Baal Aruch, without Yod, מרמטה. But the true reading is מרמוטה marmota: as this animal is called in the Alps themselves, an animal than which not even the dormouse is sleepier. Scaliger, On Subtlety, Exercise 203: They (the marmots) agree with the dormouse kind in sleep. For they pass whole winter months in torpor. Gesner: These mice sleep a great deal, and lie hidden in their burrows, which they dig with wonderful skill, etc. Agricola: It indulges very much in sleep, etc. In the mountains they gather the hay that grows softest among the rocks and carry it into the burrow, so that they may sleep more softly in winter. Stumpf, in the Chronicles of Switzerland: For the sake of food they are dug out only in winter, while asleep. Likewise: And having dug up the earth, they carry them off asleep. And a little later: when the place is dug up, they are found asleep, etc., and they are carried asleep wherever one pleases. For they do not easily wake up unless the heat of the sun, of a fire or of a stove has loosened them. And again: They are even killed while still asleep, by driving a knife into the throat, whereupon they begin to move their forefeet a little. But they expire before they are fully awake. And long before, Pliny, the only one of the ancients who mentions this mouse, book 8, chapter 37: In winter [II, 416] the Pontic mice also hide away, etc. The Alpine ones also hide away. That is, to sleep deeply in their burrows. Therefore the sleep of Saul and of the soldiers around him, who slept so deeply that they did not notice David and Abishai advancing right up to the royal tent and carrying off Saul's spear, is rightly called by the Hebrew writer תרדמת מרמוטה, the sleep of the marmot.
